subject: comm
source: CIPM Intermediate I Practice Question Bank

questions.q: Listening, as distinguished from hearing, is best described as:
opts: A passive physical process requiring no attention
An active mental process requiring attention, involving the ears, eyes and brain
Identical in every respect to hearing
A skill that cannot be improved with practice

questions.q: The key distinction between hearing and listening is that:
opts: Hearing ascribes sense and meaning to a message, while listening does not
Hearing is merely reception of speech sounds, while listening ascribes sense, meaning and context to the message
There is no meaningful distinction between the two
Hearing only occurs in formal settings

questions.q: An individual hearing a conversation in their presence without being directly involved or needing to respond, as at a social gathering, is engaged in:
opts: Active listening
Empathetic listening
Critical listening
Casual listening

questions.q: Active (focused) listening is best described as:
opts: Listening with a purpose
Listening without any specific aim
Listening only to formal speeches
A synonym for casual listening

questions.q: 'Pseudo-listening' refers to:
opts: A highly effective listening technique
The listener appearing to listen while having actually 'switched off' concentration
A formal listening assessment method
Listening exclusively to written text

questions.q: Which is identified as a barrier to effective listening?
opts: Emotional problems such as anger, fear, hatred and prejudice
Maintaining eye contact with the speaker
Taking brief notes during a talk
Sitting where you can see the speaker clearly

questions.q: A good listener is one who:
opts: Interrupts frequently to demonstrate engagement
Is patient, pays careful attention to detail, and is not in haste to interrupt the speaker
Focuses only on formulating their own response
Avoids eye contact to concentrate better

questions.q: Reading comprehension is best defined as:
opts: The physical act of moving one's eyes across a page
The ability to read and interpret a written text
A skill unrelated to vocabulary development
Exclusively the memorisation of a text word-for-word

questions.q: Comprehension is best understood as:
opts: The input of reading, while reading itself is the output
The output of reading, while reading itself is the input
Identical in meaning to vocabulary
Unrelated to the reading process

questions.q: Drawing inferences, as a task in reading comprehension, involves:
opts: Copying the text verbatim
Reasoning to determine facts not overtly/directly stated in the text
Ignoring the context of a passage entirely
Reading only the introduction of a passage

questions.q: The denotative meaning of a word refers to:
opts: Its ordinary or literal (dictionary) meaning
Its emotional or implied association only
A meaning that changes with every context
A meaning found only in poetry

questions.q: 'Skimming' as a reading technique involves:
opts: Reading every word slowly and carefully
Reading the passage quickly to grasp the general idea
Re-reading a passage multiple times for detail
Reading aloud to oneself

questions.q: 'Scanning' as a reading technique involves:
opts: Reading for pure entertainment only
Careful reading through a text for specific details, then extracting needed information
Skipping the text entirely
Reading only the first and last paragraphs

questions.q: 'Regression', as a bad reading habit, refers to:
opts: Reading at an increasingly faster pace
Re-reading portions of a text already read, wasting time and indicating lack of concentration
Reading silently with no lip movement
Skimming a text for its general idea

questions.q: 'Vocalisation', as a bad reading habit, refers to:
opts: Reading silently with no sound
Pronouncing words audibly while reading
Reading unusually fast
Reading only technical material

questions.q: 'Sub-vocalisation', as a bad reading habit, refers to:
opts: Reading aloud so others can hear
Unconsciously moving the lips and pronouncing words without audible sound
Skipping difficult words entirely
Reading a text twice for comprehension

questions.q: A narrow eye span, as a bad reading habit, results in:
opts: Faster reading with better comprehension
Restricting the reader's focus to one word at a time, slowing reading pace
No measurable effect on reading speed
Improved retention of the material

questions.q: Writing, in the context of this chapter, is best described as:
opts: A purely mechanical skill with no creative element
An art — the ability to use writing symbols to express ideas, feelings or thoughts in a meaningful, retrievable form
A skill that cannot be taught or improved
Identical in every way to speaking

questions.q: The process of writing consists of how many stages?
opts: Four: prewriting, writing, revising and proofreading
Only one: writing
Two: reading and writing
Six: unrelated to prewriting or revising

questions.q: 'Outlining', in the prewriting stage, refers to:
opts: The final proofreading step
Organising ideas into a structured plan before drafting
Publishing the finished document
A synonym for revising

questions.q: A paragraph is best defined as:
opts: A single word standing alone
A unit of discourse built around one central idea
A list with no coherent theme
Always exactly five sentences long

questions.q: The topic sentence of a paragraph is best described as:
opts: The sentence stating in general terms the central idea of the paragraph
Always the final sentence of a paragraph
A sentence that introduces an unrelated idea
Optional and rarely used in formal writing

questions.q: Note-taking, as a communication skill, allows a writer to:
opts: Aid memory and provide material for later consultation
Avoid the need to listen at all
Replace formal minutes entirely
Guarantee zero errors in writing

questions.q: Which of the following commonly reinforces a speaker's message during a speech?
opts: Nodding, proverbs, and body gestures
Complete stillness with no movement at all
Reading directly from a script with no eye contact
Speaking in monotone throughout

questions.q: A speaker can best maintain rapport with an audience by:
opts: Pacing up and down continuously
Maintaining eye contact with the audience
Asking questions repeatedly without pause
Winking occasionally at audience members

questions.q: Intonation in speech could expose a speaker's:
opts: Feelings
Past employment history
Facial expression alone
Handwriting style

questions.q: To make a speech interesting, speakers are generally advised to avoid:
opts: Jokes
Proverbs
Jargon
Illustrations

questions.q: 'Equipment' is grammatically classified as:
opts: A count (countable) noun that should be pluralised as 'equipments'
A non-count (uncountable) noun that should not be pluralised
A proper noun requiring capitalisation
A verb rather than a noun

questions.q: 'News' is grammatically classified as:
opts: An uncountable noun that should not be preceded by the indefinite article 'a'
A countable noun requiring 'a' before it
A verb describing the act of reporting
A plural noun requiring a plural verb

questions.q: A 'homonym' is best defined as a word with:
opts: Multiple spellings but one fixed meaning
The same pronunciation and spelling as another word, but a different meaning
No relationship to any other word in the language
Only one possible pronunciation across all dialects

questions.q: 'Polysemy' refers to:
opts: A word with only one possible meaning
The multiplicity of meanings a single word may carry, disambiguated by context
A grammatical error common in Nigerian English
The use of two words with identical spelling only

questions.q: 'Furniture' is grammatically classified, per the chapter, as:
opts: A countable noun always requiring a plural form
An uncountable (non-count) noun
A proper noun
A verb

questions.q: In reported/indirect speech, tense generally shifts:
opts: Forward (e.g. 'was' becomes 'is')
Backward (e.g. 'is' becomes 'was')
Not at all, regardless of context
Only in questions, never in statements

questions.q: A semicolon, among punctuation marks, is most appropriately used to:
opts: End a sentence definitively, like a full stop
Link closely related independent clauses
Replace a comma in every context
Indicate a direct quotation only

questions.q: A simple sentence, grammatically, is one that:
opts: Contains two or more independent clauses joined by 'and'
Contains one independent clause (one subject-verb unit)
Always contains a dependent clause
Cannot stand alone as a complete thought

questions.q: A complex sentence, grammatically, is one that contains:
opts: Only a single independent clause
One independent clause plus one or more dependent (subordinate) clauses
Two independent clauses with no subordination
No verb at all

questions.q: In subject-verb concord, a compound subject joined by 'and' (e.g. 'John and Mary') generally takes a:
opts: Singular verb
Plural verb
No verb at all
Verb that depends solely on which noun appears first

questions.q: A business letter, as distinguished from a personal letter, is one that:
opts: Emanates from a business organisation or individual and deals with a business issue, in a strictly formal tone
Is always handwritten rather than typed
Never requires a signature
Is addressed only to government agencies

questions.q: A complaint letter is written to:
opts: Formally raise dissatisfaction about an issue, such as delayed delivery, while preserving the business relationship
Permanently end a business relationship with no further contact
Request a job interview
Announce a company's annual profits

questions.q: A memo, unlike a formal business letter, typically:
opts: Includes a full salutation and complimentary close
Lacks a salutation and complimentary close, and is brief and strictly official
Is always sent to external clients only
Requires a notarised signature

questions.q: The standard heading elements of a memo typically include:
opts: From, To, Date and Subject Matter
Only a subject line, with no sender or date
A complimentary close and signature block only
A postage stamp and envelope address

questions.q: A circular, as a form of business correspondence, is generally used by:
opts: A single junior employee addressing their direct supervisor only
Top management, to convey policies, directives and new developments to the entire workforce
External customers to lodge complaints
Government agencies exclusively

questions.q: A statutory meeting is one that is held because it is:
opts: Purely optional and informal
Required according to the rules and regulations of an organisation
Called only in a crisis with no advance notice
Attended exclusively by external auditors

questions.q: Minutes of a meeting are best described as:
opts: A verbatim word-for-word transcript of everything said
The official, concise written record of matters discussed and decisions reached
An informal personal opinion of the meeting's chairperson
A document written before the meeting takes place

questions.q: The grapevine, as an informal communication channel, is best described as:
opts: An official, fully traceable means of communication approved by management
An unofficial, usually baseless and anonymous means of disseminating information (hearsay/gossip)
A synonym for a formal memo
A channel used exclusively by senior management

questions.q: A key weakness of grapevine communication is that it:
opts: Is always completely accurate and verifiable
Is usually fallacious, and even where partially true, is often doctored, distorted or embellished
Follows the organisation's official hierarchy strictly
Moves more slowly than formal communication channels

questions.q: Management's best response to workplace rumours, per the chapter, is to:
opts: Respond publicly to every single rumour regardless of significance
Not respond to every trivial rumour, since over-reacting can undermine management's standing
Ignore all rumours permanently with no exceptions
Fire any employee suspected of starting a rumour

questions.q: Cross-cultural communication barriers commonly arise from differences in:
opts: Language, values, and non-verbal cues such as gestures
Only the time zone of the parties involved
Only the currency used by each party
Font choice in written correspondence

questions.q: Conflict in an organisational setting is best understood as:
opts: Always destructive, with no possible benefit to the organisation
A disagreement that, if managed constructively, can also produce positive organisational change
A phenomenon that occurs only between employees of equal rank
Something that can be entirely eliminated through good management
